name: Kebra Nagast
info: The Kebra Nagast, or Glory of the Kings, is a 14th-century Ethiopian national epic in Geʽez that traces the Solomonic dynasty to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through Menelik I and tells how the Ark of the Covenant came to Ethiopia.

facts.made: Attributed to Nebure Id Yeshaq of Aksum; its colophon names a team of Ethiopian clerics who translated it into Geʽez from Arabic, in a tradition that gives Coptic as the first language
facts.form: A composite prose work in Geʽez, divided into 117 chapters and framed as a debate of the 318 fathers of the First Council of Nicaea
facts.where: Copies are held in libraries, among them a manuscript at the Bodleian Library (shelfmark Bruce 87), which James Bruce brought from Gondar
facts.known: The Queen of Sheba (Makeda) and Solomon; Menelik I; the Ark of the Covenant coming to Ethiopia; the Solomonic dynasty's claimed descent; the debate of the 318 fathers; prophecies of Ethiopia's power

t: The text traces the Solomonic dynasty, which ruled Ethiopia until 1974, to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through their son Menelik I.
Modern scholarship considers its stories largely created to legitimise the dynasty's rise to power in the 13th century, while many Ethiopian Christians continue to regard it as historically reliable.
Its colophon gives a chain of translation from Coptic to Arabic to Geʽez, but many scholars doubt that a Coptic version ever existed.
dyk: In the story, Menelik asked Solomon for only a single tassel from the cloth covering the Ark of the Covenant, and Solomon gave him the entire thing; the young men travelling with him then smuggled the Ark out of the Temple.
ev: The Arabic translation named in the colophon is dated to this year

sections.origins:
The Kebra Nagast, or The Glory of the Kings, is a national epic of Ethiopia written in Geʽez. It purports to trace the origins of the Solomonic dynasty, the line of Ethiopian Orthodox Christian monarchs who ruled the country until 1974, to the biblical king Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through Menelik I. Modern scholarship considers its stories to have been largely created to legitimise the dynasty's rise to power in Ethiopia in the 13th century, and it enabled the overthrow of the Zagwe dynasty. The historian Stuart Munro-Hay stated that there is no record of Ethiopian monarchs claiming descent from Solomon before the 13th century.

Several explanations have been offered for the Solomonic idea. The central Solomonic narrative is thought to derive from the Zagwe dynasty, who believed the Axumites were descended from Solomon. The myth might be rooted in half remembered oral traditions of an ancient Eurasian back migration into Ethiopia, or it may reflect a sort of Axumite philosemitism, with Ezana calling himself a follower of the "god of Israel" and a later king named Israel of Axum. The Roman Jewish historian Josephus, in a 1st-century account, identified Solomon's visitor as a queen of Egypt and Ethiopia.
sections.content:
The Kebra Nagast is divided into 117 chapters and is clearly a composite work; Edward Ullendorff describes its narrative as "a gigantic conflation of legendary cycles". It draws much of its material from the Hebrew Bible and is presented as a debate among the 318 "orthodox fathers" of the First Council of Nicaea, who ask "Of what doth the Glory of Kings consist?" One Gregory answers in a speech that ends with the statement that a copy of the Glory of God was made by Moses and kept in the Ark of the Covenant. The archbishop Dĕmâtĕyôs then reads from a book he had found in the church of "Sophia", which introduces what David Allan Hubbard calls the centrepiece of the work: the story of Makeda, Solomon, Menelik I and how the Ark came to Ethiopia (chapters 19 to 94).

In that story Queen Makeda learns of Solomon's wisdom from a merchant, Tamrin, travels to Jerusalem and declares that she will worship the Creator of the sun, the God of Israel. Solomon tricks her into sleeping with him and gives her a ring; she gives birth to Menelik on the way home. At 22 Menelik travels to Jerusalem and returns with a company of the first-born sons of the elders, who smuggle the Ark out of the Temple without his knowledge. Menelik and his entourage are miraculously flown home, and at Axum Makeda abdicates in his favour. The closing chapters are prophecies with a marked anti-Jewish attitude, ending with the power of Rome eclipsed by that of Ethiopia and king Kaleb of Axum subduing the Jews of Najran.
sections.making:
According to the colophon attached to most of the existing copies, the Kebra Nagast was originally written in Coptic, translated into Arabic in the "year of mercy" 409 (dated to AD 1225), and then into Geʽez by a team of clerics in Ethiopia during the office of Abuna Abba Giyorgis, possibly at the command of the governor of Enderta, Ya'ibika Igzi'. On the testimony of this colophon, Conti Rossini, Littmann and Cerulli, among others, marked off the period 1314 to 1321–1322 for the composition. Other sources put it as a work of the fourteenth-century Nebura'ed Yeshaq of Aksum.

Some historians have been suspicious of the colophon and have suggested that the authors of the original text were Ethiopian scribes. Careful study has revealed traces of Arabic, possibly pointing to an Arabic prior version, but no clear evidence of a Coptic one, and many scholars doubt that a Coptic version ever existed. The many Bible quotations were copied from the Ethiopian translation of the Bible, directly or from memory. Hubbard alleged patristic, Qur'anic, rabbinical and apocryphal sources, among them the Book of Enoch and the Book of Jubilees; Marcus describes the work as "a pastiche of legends". Other historians consider parts of it to date as late as the end of the sixteenth century.
sections.reception:
Edward Ullendorff, in the 1967 Schweich Lectures, wrote that "The Kebra Nagast is not merely a literary work, but it is the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings". Nadia Nurhussein wrote that it gave textual authority to a then newly articulated mythology of Abyssinia's long imperial history, legitimising a "Solomonic" dynasty that claimed to reach back three thousand years earlier to the union of Solomon and the supposedly Ethiopian Queen of Sheba. Many Ethiopian Christians continue to believe it is a historically reliable work. It has also been described as "an Abyssinian politico-religious epic" and as "medieval-era mythology".

Modern scholarly consensus is that there is no historical evidence supporting the legends of the claimed origins of the Solomonic dynasty. By this view there is no credible basis to the claims that the Aksumite royal house descended from Solomon, or that any Aksumite king even claimed such an ancestry, or that Yekuno Amlak, the 13th-century founder of the dynasty, descended from the Aksumite royal house. Solomon is dated to the 10th century BCE, hundreds of years before the founding of Aksum. Harold Marcus holds that the stories were created to legitimise Yekuno Amlak's seizure of power, and David Northrup notes that the line of descent is highly improbable and unsupported by evidence.
sections.survival:
Information on the Kebra Nagast reached Europe through the Jesuits. Pedro Páez included a detailed translation of the text through Menelek's return to Aksum with the Ark of the Covenant in his História da Ethiópia, completed in the early 1620s but not published in his lifetime. It provided the foundation for many later Jesuit accounts, including those of Manuel de Almeida and Balthazar Telles. Almeida, who had an excellent command of the language, added more in his Historia de Etiopía. In the first quarter of the 16th century P.N. Godinho published some traditions about Solomon and Menelik derived from the text, and Baltazar Téllez (1595–1675) supplied further information in his Historia General de Etiopía Alta (Coimbra, 1660).

Its contents became generally known among European scholars and theologians only at the close of the eighteenth century, when the Scottish travel writer James Bruce of Kinnaird published his travels. Ras Mikael Sehul had given him a copy as he left Gondar, and a description of its contents appeared in the third edition of 1813; the documents were later given to the Bodleian Library (shelfmark Bruce 87). August Dillmann summarised the contents and published the colophon, and F. Praetorius published chapters 19 to 32 with a Latin translation. Carl Bezold published the entire text with commentary in 1905, and the first English translation, by E. A. Wallis Budge, appeared in two editions, in 1922 and 1932.
sections.legacy:
The text gave the Solomonic dynasty, which ruled Ethiopia until 1974, a descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and so a place in the Davidic line from which Jesus was also descended. Ullendorff called it the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings. Its account of the conversion of Ethiopians from the worship of the Sun, Moon and stars to that of the "Lord God of Israel", and of the Ark's arrival with Menelik I, became part of that national memory.

The Ethiopian regnal list of 1922 takes much from the national epic. It claims that an "Ag'azyan" dynasty reigned from 1985 to 982 BCE, founded by a man named Akbunas Saba (Sheba) "of the posterity of the kingdom of Joctan", a descendant of Shem, with Makeda as the last ruler of the line. This regnal list is not considered historically accurate and has been treated by historians as little more than a vague notion of historical tradition in Northeast Africa. Agazi, the founder of the eponymous dynasty, is said to have slain the serpent Arwe, a deed that the Kebra Nagast credits to Menelik I.

summary: The Kebra Nagast is a 14th-century Ethiopian epic in Geʽez that traces the Solomonic dynasty to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba and tells how the Ark of the Covenant reached Ethiopia. Scholars hold that its stories legitimised the dynasty's 13th-century rise, while many Ethiopian Christians regard it as historically reliable.

notes: Dating: the article gives the colophon's chain (Coptic, Arabic dated AD 1225, Geʽez), the 1314 to 1321-1322 period marked off by Conti Rossini, Littmann and Cerulli, authorship by Nebure Id Yeshaq of Aksum in the 14th century, and other historians who date parts as late as the end of the 16th century. start 1314 is the beginning of the first period; circa true.

The article says the Kebra Nagast was 'at least 700 years old' in its existing form and calls the author 'Nebura'ed Yeshaq' in one place and 'Nebure Id Yeshaq' in another; the text uses the article's spellings in each place.

Left out: the Gregory identification (Thaumaturgus vs the Illuminator), the Stories of Kings chapter details, the Sabaean mlkt/mqtwyt etymology of Makeda, Kropp's remarks on the Ag'azyan spelling and the Alaqa Taye/Heruy accounts of Joktan's sons (garbled passage), the Prester John print of 1533 (not about this text), Almeida's brother's death, Leeman's article.
The article's survival section has no manuscript list beyond the Bruce copy at the Bodleian.
